rss.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
rss.summary: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234 Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this , and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. 3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14 Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: uv self update Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: uv python install 3.15 And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: uv python pin --global 3.15 Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: uv run python --version I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15 Then I can confirm the version like this: datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq Highlights from Python 3.11 The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported . My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio . 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout() , and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc . Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python. create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step() , value() , inverse() , and finalize() methods. blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row. You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this! Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system . I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. I've also updated my click-app , datasette-plugin , python-lib , and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15. rss.summary: A healthcare professional sits at a desk reviewing mammogram scans and medical diagrams on dual computer monitors.

Google’s health research and tools span from fundamental cellular discovery to laboratory analysis and patient impact. Over the last five years, Google teams have published 90 peer-reviewed research papers about understanding and addressing diseases, accumulating more than 90,000 citations. And building on our vision for how technology can accelerate science to improve lives , we’re collaborating with clinicians, academic institutes, and researchers to ensure discoveries make it out of the lab to benefit patients. Here is how our efforts are helping to advance medical research and public health solutions. Decoding the mechanics of disease AlphaGenome Atlas is the most comprehensive catalog of predictions for how single-letter variant changes in the human genome affect molecular biology. To effectively treat an illness, it helps to understand how it operates at the molecular, genetic, and cellular levels. Our early-stage biology models act as collaborative research tools for scientists, revealing nature's hidden mechanics and advancing medical discoveries. Accelerating drug discovery: Researchers at the Institute for Global Health, Barcelona, used AlphaFold to virtually screen 30,000 compounds for antiparasitic activity against Chagas disease, a neglected tropical illness that affects roughly 8 million people and can lead to life-threatening complications if left untreated. This research helped the Institute identify two FDA-approved drugs that could be repurposed for Chagas, expediting time-to-treatment. Mapping genetic variants linked to aging: Identifying which rare genetic changes are linked to specific diseases is challenging because the volume of non-impactful mutations creates "background noise." rss.title: Dwarf Fortress uses version control now
rss.summary: I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more . That's art. I went looking and I'm sad to report that the days without version control appear to have ended. Quoting Tarn Adams over time: March 2013: "I don't use version control -- I didn't like the feeling of having the code get committed into a black box thingy with no immediate upside" March 2016: "I don’t even use version control. If you don’t know what that is then you’re not gonna yell at me. If you even know what version control is you’re gonna be like, ‘You don’t use version control? You don’t use source control? What is wrong with you? How can you even work? I’m just not cut out for it, in a sense. It’s been 15 years, so the reasons have change over time, but that’s my current understanding of it." March 2023: "I've got Discord channels to check and version control stuff to use now, so the process is definitely a little more involved" That March 2023 quote comes from an interview about the release on Steam which made them millionaires . I'm a tiny bit sad that they gave in before they hit that milestone, but what an impressive run. Tags: version-control

github.description: TokenSpeed is a speed-of-light LLM inference engine.
github.text_excerpt: TokenSpeed is a speed-of-light LLM inference engine designed for **agentic workloads**, with TensorRT-LLM-level performance and vLLM-level usability. The goal is to be the most performant inference engine for production agentic workloads. Core components: - **Scheduler**: C++ control plane and Python execution plane. Request lifecycle, KV cache ownership, and overlap timing are encoded as a finite-state machine, with safe KV resource reuse enforced by the type system at compile time. - **Kernels**: pluggable, layered kernel system with a portable public API and a centralized registry including one of the fastest **MLA** (Multi-head Latent Attention) implementations on Blackwell for agentic workloads. - **Entrypoint**: SMG-integrated AsyncLLM for low-overhead CPU-side request handling. ## Differentiation TokenSpeed takes a fundamentally different architectural approach from existing LLM inference engines. The **PyTorch Foundation highlighted these architectural differentiators** when [welcoming TokenSpeed](https://pytorch.org/blog/pytorch-ecosystem-landscape-q3-update/) to the PyTorch Ecosystem Landscape: > TokenSpeed is an open source LLM inference engine and the first to separate the control plane from the execution plane. The control plane is implemented in C++ as a finite-state machine, using the type system to enforce safe resource management, including request lifecycles and KV cache state, at compile time rather than runtime. The execution plane is implemented in Python, enabling fast iteration and lowering the cognitive load for researchers and engineers. This architecture combines strong correctness guarantees in the core scheduling system with the development velocity of a high-level execution layer. > > TokenSpeed also treats kernels as a first-class, modular subsystem, separating them from the core engine through a portable public API, centralized registry and selection model, and an extensible plugin mechanism for heterogeneous accelerators. # senpi

> ⚠️ **Experimental.** senpi is an opinionated, in-flight fork of [badlogic/pi-mono](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono). It powers [Dori](https://sisyphuslabs.ai) under the hood and reflects what one specific AI assistant needs from a coding-agent runtime. Use it; don't bet a production pipeline on it. senpi is a senpai-name pun and a more **sane** pi with extra batteries included — a TypeScript monorepo that rebrands pi-mono's coding agent as `senpi` and ships a curated set of builtin extensions and core tweaks on top of upstream. > **Upstream**: [pi-mono](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) by [@mariozechner](https://github.com/badlogic) — tools for building AI agents and managing LLM deployments. ## Inspired by OMO, built as Dori's coding-agent runtime senpi was born from two influences: - **Strong influence from [OMO (oh-my-openagent)](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent).** OMO is the heavyweight opencode harness with discipline agents (Sisyphus, Hephaestus, Prometheus), [IntentGate](https://factory.ai/news/terminal-bench), hash-anchored edits, Team Mode, skill-embedded MCPs, Ralph Loop, todo enforcers, and a lot more. senpi reuses many of OMO's signature ideas (intent gate, dynamic prompt, per-model presets, parallel-tool routing, todo continuation) but **keeps the surface as light as possible** so it can stay close to upstream pi-mono. Think of senpi as **a light version of OMO** that runs as a single pi CLI binary instead of an opencode plugin. - **senpi is the coding-agent runtime for [Dori](https://sisyphuslabs.ai).** Dori is Sisyphus Labs' AI assistant — see the [Dori callout in OMO's README](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent#oh-my-openagent) for context. senpi is usable standalone, but the design decisions (intent gate phrasing, builtin extension set, prompt presets per model family, branding) are tuned for what Dori needs when it executes code work. Render them, edit them, diff them, and hand them to an agent — from .NET, the browser, Python, or the shell.

aihot.summary: AWS 团队发布论文《Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers》，提出 priming 方法，复用预训练 Transformer 权重构建混合架构，将预训练成本降低逾 99%，全流程消耗不足源模型 0.5% 的 token 预算。
aihot.text_excerpt:
AI agents are rapidly scaling: longer sessions, deeper reasoning chains, more autonomy. But the Transformer architecture underneath them still pays a memory tax that grows with the number of tokens it processes. As agents become more capable, that cost scales with them. Now, there’s a proliferation of hybrid architectures that use some combination of methods to achieve a better balance of memory, speed, and quality. Those methods include sparse attention, which selects a subset of past tokens to consider when selecting the next token; sliding-window attention, which preserves only the most recent tokens; and state space models, which compress information from the full history into a fixed-size state. These hybrid architectures can be understood as points in a sequence-model design space: to differing degrees, they mix information while traversing a sequence and passing through different states. What distinguishes them from each other is how they retain and use the past. Until now, exploring this design space has required training every new architecture from scratch, using trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. This has made controlled comparisons of hybrid architectures extremely expensive. In a new paper, “ Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers ,” our team at Amazon Web Services addresses this problem. We introduce priming, a method that leverages pretrained Transformer weights as a starting point to reduce the pretraining cost of hybrid architectures by more than 99%. With priming, model developers can ask questions that were previously too expensive to answer at scale: Which attention layers can be replaced by more-efficient layers? How many attention layers can be replaced without sacrificing quality? Which state space layer works best? And what does the trade-off between speed and accuracy look like? In our paper, we compare hybrid models that use three different types of state space models (Gated KalmaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2). Some of our findings: Not all state space models are equal. Under controlled conditions, Gated KalmaNet (GKA) performs best, followed by Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and then Mamba-2. aihot.text_excerpt: Google Deepmind's AI solved dozens of open math problems on its own, per a new study in Science . AlphaProof Nexus cracked nine of 353 open Erdős problems, two unsolved for 56 years. The team shared those solutions online ahead of the paper. Beyond that, AlphaProof Nexus proved 44 conjectures from the OEIS integer sequence database, solved an open question in algebraic geometry, and improved a known bound in min-max optimization, a technique used to train some AI models. It's built around Gemini 3.1 Pro, which drafts and revises proofs in the formal language Lean. Lean checks each draft after every edit, and error messages guide the next attempt. For harder sub-problems, it can call on AlphaProof , a specialized proof tool. Even without AlphaProof, it solved the nine Erdős problems, Google Deepmind reports . The study lands amid a heated debate over AI math. OpenAI recently dumped hundreds of AI proofs on GitHub instead of submitting them to journals. The Association for Human Mathematics, led by Terence Tao, called for a boycott . Deepmind put its work through peer review. aihot.text_excerpt:
In recent months, we’ve made substantial progress on reducing the effectiveness of distillation attacks on Claude using new methods, as we outline in this blog. Early evidence suggests that these methods have reduced the amount of data harvested by distillers by around 90 to 99 percent. Distillation attacks are covert, industrial-scale campaigns to extract the capabilities of one model and replicate them in another, without the authorization of the original model’s developers. They are often conducted using networks of fraudulent accounts. These attacks allow companies to mimic frontier capabilities for a fraction of the development time and cost. aihot.text_excerpt: IT之家 10 月 10 日消息，据《纽约时报》当地时间 9 日报道，Anthropic 披露，旗下 AI 智能体 曾在无人指示的情况下 ，试图访问美国联邦、州及地方政府的多个网站。Anthropic 没有公布涉及的政府机构名称，已向白宫通报这些事件。 Anthropic 在博客文章中提到，一款处于测试阶段的 AI 模型 擅自执行了多项操作 ，包括利用某大学网站的漏洞下载数据，以及向某政府机构提交一份原本被明确禁止提交的表格。 Anthropic 在审查旗下 AI 于 7 月的操作记录时发现了这些问题。当时，OpenAI 披露旗下 AI 技术曾攻击初创企业 Hugging Face，Anthropic 及其他 AI 实验室也发现，旗下 AI 曾脱离测试环境，实施黑客攻击。 Anthropic 一名发言人拒绝就博客文章之外的内容发表评论。 当天早些时候，费城警察局披露，Anthropic 曾通知警方，旗下 AI 通过警方网站提交了一条虚假的凶杀案线索。警方称，举报日期为 7 月 18 日，提交者声称掌握一起尚未侦破案件的线索。 警方将举报标记为垃圾信息，没有展开调查。IT之家从报道中获悉，Anthropic 本周向费城警方通报了此事，并告知警方将在周五公开披露。 Anthropic 解释道，一款尚未发布的非前沿研究模型原本需要填写一份模拟政府表格。但由于模拟表格加载失败，或者模型误将表格关闭，模型转而进入提供正式表格的网站，并提交了表格。
